entries.title: Trump official claims record-breaking 300,000 visas were revoked
entries.summary: The revocations targeted US visa holders who had allegedly broken the law, a spokesperson said.
entries.content:
The revocations targeted visa holders who had allegedly broken the law, or pose threats to national security.

The Trump administration has said it has revoked more than 300,000 visas issued to foreign nationals, claiming it has done so at a faster pace than any previous administration.

A spokesman for the US Department of State said on social media on Tuesday that the revocations targeted foreign nationals in the United States on visas who had broken the law, committed fraud or posed threats to national security.

“We have zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law, commit fraud, or undermine our national security,” Tommy Pigott, State Department spokesman, said in a post on the social media platform X.

The administration would continue taking action to secure US borders and protect national security, he added.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the State Department for comment.

The number of visa revocations exceeded 175,000 in August.

In January, the department said it had revoked more than 100,000 visas, a record at the time.

The administration has also adopted a stricter policy on granting visas, with tightened social media vetting and expanded screening.

Rights advocates and human rights experts have condemned the Trump administration’s social media screening efforts, which they say threaten free speech and are akin to surveillance and the singling out of immigrants.

entries.title: Lavrov backs Tehran, but does Russia also gain from the US-Iran crisis?
entries.summary: Moscow pledges support to its sanctioned ally, but analysts say the war Iran wants to end has filled Russia’s coffers.
entries.content:
Moscow pledges support to its sanctioned ally, but analysts say the war that Iran wants to end has filled Russia’s coffers.

Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov pledged Moscow’s support for Iran when he met his counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, and President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran on Monday.

On Tuesday, Araghchi wrote on X: “Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now.”

But Russia’s position is not straightforward.

The war on Iran, launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, has pushed up oil prices and handed Moscow a windfall. Washington has now also eased sanctions on Russian energy to bring down fuel costs – a major complaint from consumers in the US, who will shortly vote in mid-term elections.

So how close are Moscow and Tehran, and does Russia really want the US-Iran crisis to end? Here’s what you need to know:

Why has Lavrov visited Tehran now?

To shore up a wartime partnership, and to shape what happens next.

Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera that with both countries fighting wars, Lavrov’s “primary motive is to solidify that alliance”.

He said the aim is to advance each side’s war goals: “Russia against Ukraine, Iran against the United States.”

But Hashemi said the main reason is that the US-Israeli attack has left the Middle East regional order unravelling, and Moscow wants a say in what replaces it.

“I suspect there’s a longer-term agenda here,” he said.

How close are Russia and Iran?

They have a strategic partnership, though their treaty stops short of a military alliance.

Putin and Pezeshkian signed a 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in Moscow in January 2025.

It came into force that October, but unlike Russia’s pact with North Korea, it has no mutual defence clause.

Ties deepened after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with Iran sharing Shahed drone technology that enabled Russia to build its own version.

In 2024, Washington accused Tehran of also sending Russia ballistic missiles.

In Tehran, Lavrov said Russian specialists who had left Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant – heavily damaged in US strikes – would gradually return.

Other countries are aware of the closeness of their relationship.

On Sunday, Lavrov was in Bahrain for a strategic dialogue session between Russia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), and he was urged by its members to use Moscow’s influence with Tehran to press for “serious dialogue” and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic Gulf waterway that Iran effectively closed shortly after the war began earlier this year.

Has Russia helped Iran in the war against the US?

Not openly.

The Russian Foreign Ministry has condemned what it called the “unlawful aggression” of the US and Israel, but Moscow has not intervened militarily.

US media outlets, citing intelligence reports, have said Russia and China supplied Iran with satellite imagery and weapons components. US President Donald Trump has dismissed those reports.

How has Russia benefitted from the US-Iran war?

Significantly.

After Iran effectively closed Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas supplies are shipped during peacetime, the price of Brent crude rose from around $72 a barrel to as high as $120 a barrel in March and April. On Tuesday, Brent – the global benchmark – was trading at above $109 a barrel.

By April, revenue from Russia’s biggest oil tax had roughly doubled to about $9bn, according to Reuters calculations, as buyers unable to get supplies from the Gulf switched.

Since March, the US Treasury has issued waivers allowing sales of Russian oil already loaded at sea. This month, it waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027.

On Friday, Trump suspended newly passed sanctions on Russia and on buyers of its oil and gas. The move has sparked outrage among members of his own Republican Party who backed the sanctions bill.

On Sunday, he claimed he did not want to “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table” in Ukraine talks.

“The Kremlin is using this opportunity to align Russian and American interests on Ukraine to try to stop Ukraine from continuing its attacks on Russian refineries,” John Lough, an associate fellow of the Russia and Eurasia Programme at Chatham House and a senior research fellow at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, told Al Jazeera.

“This has led to the breakdown of relations between Trump and Zelenskyy, which suits Moscow’s purposes because it is putting US policy in conflict with Europe’s policy on Ukraine,” he said.

So, does Russia really want the US-Iran war to end?

For now, Russia would appear to have every reason to want the stand-off between Washington and Tehran to continue, as it is “benefiting from higher oil prices and from the diesel squeeze that has encouraged Trump to lift sanctions and allow Russia to supply diesel to the US market,” Lough said.

But Nikita Smagin, an analyst on Russia’s role in the Middle East, told Al Jazeera on Monday that while Russia certainly has a partial interest in the conflict continuing, on balance, it likely does not want to see it escalate, as the consequences could be unpredictable.

Could Russia be an effective mediator in the US-Iran war?

Moscow talks to all sides caught up in this conflict, which Hashemi said gives it an edge over Washington. Much of the region has been affected as Iran has launched strikes against US military assets and energy infrastructure in the countries hosting US assets. These include Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.

Hashemi said Russia is “perfectly situated to shape a future new Middle East regional order” as “a major power that has direct diplomatic relations with all of the parties” in the region.

“The United States can’t make that claim because the United States has no relationship with Iran,” he said.

Putin has already acted as a channel with Washington, stating he relayed Iran’s views on ending the conflict to Trump in a phone call on October 9.

But Hashemi said he did not think “Trump is looking to Putin to help solve the Iran war”.

Trump’s Iran policy is shaped, he said, “first and foremost by Trump’s personal idiosyncrasies”, and then by his relationship with Israel, reflected among close advisers including Jared Kushner, Steve Witkoff and Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the United Nations.

Still, with Trump “in a quagmire”, Hashemi added: “I suspect that there are intense discussions between Russia and the United States.”

That could come to a head at a possible three-way summit.

Last month, the Kremlin said Putin and Trump had discussed meeting China’s President Xi Jinping to talk about the Ukraine war, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen in November, but the White House has not confirmed whether Trump will attend.

If such a meeting on Ukraine goes ahead, Hashemi said he suspects “the Iran war will also be part of the discussion”, with Trump looking to China and Russia “to see whether there’s any room there to help him negotiate an end to the war”.

What happens next?

On Monday, Lavrov said Moscow expects Pezeshkian to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow at the end of October.

Meanwhile, US and Iranian forces continue to fight for control of Hormuz ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.

Trump has threatened to “soon finish the job” with Iran, but Araghchi responded by saying, “We have unfinished jobs, too.”

entries.title: ‘You have to sacrifice’: Trump voters stay loyal as US midterms approach
entries.summary: Rising economic pain confronting US voters has not translated into a loss of faith among Trump’s most loyal supporters.
entries.content:
Rising economic pain confronting US voters has not translated into a loss of faith among Donald Trump’s most loyal supporters.

McConnellsburg, Pennsylvania, USA – Calvin Ott, the owner of a landscaping business in a consistent stronghold for United States President Donald Trump, is one of several so-called “MAGA voters” whose support has not wavered – even as life has gotten a lot more expensive since the president returned to office last year.

“I’m 75 years old, and I’m still working,” Ott says as he sips his Coors Light beer under the dim lights of Fulton Pub in McConnellsburg.

The pub, which serves as a watering hole for the town’s approximately 1,000 residents, is where Ott unwinds after his doctor’s appointment before making the one-hour drive back through the Appalachian Mountains to his home in Shippensburg.

“I had quadruple bypasses. I’ve had skin cancer. I have my fingers cut off. I’ve had several heart issues”, Ott said with a bit of pride, showing off his right hand that has fallen victim to decades of chainsaw and lawnmower accidents.

Despite rising medical costs – his medications have more than doubled in price since last year – and his inability to retire as he approaches his 80s, the three-time Trump voter said he will continue to vote for Republicans in next month’s US midterm elections.

“I support him 100 percent,” Ott told Al Jazeera as Foreigner’s song Urgent played in the background of the pub.

In 2016, less than 6,000 people in Fulton County, where the town is located, supported Trump’s presidential campaign. That number rose to more than 7,000 eight years later, helping to fuel Trump’s return to the White House.

For Ott, his support is less a reflection of what Trump has done than what Democrats would do if they were in power.

“He’s the only president that made a promise that he kept,” Ott said. “He hates wars, even though we’re in one. But he’s for America.”

“What the hell did Biden ever give out?” he railed about the economic policies of Trump’s Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, which included a $1,400 stimulus cheque to Americans through legislation during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Who deserves the blame?

The unrelenting support for Trump among his most loyal supporters runs through Republican strongholds like McConnellsburg.

MAGA voters like Ott make up the backbone of the president’s support: working-class, white, without college degrees, and angry with Washington.

A poll conducted last month by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17 percent of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while slightly more than a quarter of those surveyed approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Trump’s most fervent supporters say their frustrations – and economic burden – have only grown since Trump’s re-election. But unlike most Americans, they don’t blame the president for the country’s economic woes. Instead, they point to Biden, who left office last year in January.

Seated at the bar next to Ott is Rebecca Lashley, a retired nursing assistant who said Trump deserves the benefit of the doubt after Biden’s policies.

“It took Biden four years of screwing up. How’s [Trump] gonna fix it in two years?” Lashley asked.

Ott agreed.

“Do you realise what Biden left that man? He left that man a hell of a big plate”, he said.

It’s a familiar line frequently touted by the White House.

Since his return to power for a second presidential term in 2025, Trump and members of his administration have regularly claimed they aren’t to blame for the nation’s cost-of-living issues. In social media posts last month, the president wrote that “price increases throughout America were caused by Sleepy Joe Biden and the Biden Administration, not by ‘TRUMP.’”

“We’re coming out of years of energy subtraction,” US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a recent Fox News interview as he blamed the Biden administration for rising fuel prices.

Five hours south of Pennsylvania, in ruby red Amelia County, Virginia, Terry Williams largely agreed with Trump.

After cooking up a Sunday breakfast, the delivery driver sank deep into his well-worn, waterfall-back couch to prepare for a full afternoon of football viewing. But before the day’s first kickoff, he issued a blunt, expletive-laden rant about a “bullshit” economy that larger “deep state” forces were preventing the president from fixing.

“I think that Trump just [blames Biden] because he just can’t come out and tell people the truth,” the self-described “Trump-lican” said as smells of bacon grease emanated from his kitchen. “The reason why I say that is the Federal Reserve. Their answer to everything is to print money.”

“The Federal Reserve Bank, the stockholders of the Federal Reserve, whoever the hell these people are, they’re creating more currency because they don’t have no choice.”

Williams, who voiced support for Trump’s second-term pressure tactics on the Fed to lower interest rates, said policies created by the US central bank have left the country with currency that has no real intrinsic value.

“I just believe that this economy is an illusion and we’re using fake money,” he said.

‘I have to sacrifice’

After Trump campaigned on a promise to bring down stubborn inflation wrought by the pandemic, his second term has consisted of a range of broadly unpopular initiatives that have forced higher prices on much of the country.

His tariff policies, instituted during a “Liberation Day” event at the White House last year, have minimal support. The AP found that nearly 65 percent of Americans blame Trump’s policies for high costs.

The nonpartisan Tax Foundation estimates tariffs put in place under Trump resulted in an average tax increase of more than $1,000 for US households last year. After the US Supreme Court rendered most of the president’s tariffs illegal in January, that estimate is slightly lower at $820 for 2026.

The policy’s impact is felt even more acutely in Virginia, which, according to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, has paid an estimated $6.2bn extra since Trump’s tariffs were implemented. That breaks down to just under $1,800 per family.

But some of the state’s MAGA voters, like Williams, say despite the extra cost, they “believe” in Trump’s tariff policy, arguing it should be expanded.

“I love the thought of a tariff system. That way, the American people do not get taxed,” Williams said. “I love that concept.”

But it is the war in Iran that could prove to be the most consequential for Trump and Republicans when Americans make their midterm picks.

As the conflict stretches into its eighth month, just 27 percent of registered US voters said last month that they approve of it, according to a New York Times/Siena poll. That number, however, is much higher among Trump’s most loyal supporters: 65 percent.

“If it needs to happen to save our republic, absolutely,” Williams said of Trump’s war on Iran. But he expressed unease at increasing petrol prices wrought by the president’s war.

Since the first US-Israeli attack on Iran was launched in late February, fuel prices in the US have skyrocketed. The national average for regular petrol is $4.29 a gallon (3.8 litres), up more than $1.30 from last September, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

Trump has begun to acknowledge the war — and its resulting economic impacts — could cost his party control of Congress.

“Well, it’s possible,” Trump told reporters earlier this month. “Because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. So when you say, ‘Is it OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon?’, I would say 100 percent of the people say ‘no’, including worldwide. So, when you say it that way, it would help. If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”

For the sake of US security, most MAGA voters say they’re willing to bear the cost of Trump’s Iran decision — and America, they believe, should, too.

“What would happen if he wouldn’t have done that? What would happen? Nothing good,” Lashley said. “We have to sacrifice to make things better. I don’t care who you are. We’re with him to make that sacrifice.”

Ott explained how the war’s higher fuel prices have forced changes to his landscaping business. He’s had to tack a fuel surcharge onto his customers’ bills and lay off more than a dozen employees.

“I don’t have a problem with it,” Ott said about the war. “I have a business, and I have to sacrifice.”

Trump promises

President Trump has repeatedly promised that Americans will eventually reap the rewards of his policies.

After launching what turned out to be a trade war with US allies, Trump last year promised to use tariff revenue to give Americans what he described as a $2,000 “dividend” payment.

“People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump posted to his Truth Social account on November 9, before adding, “A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.”

The Trump administration had refunded more than $100bn as of late August following the Supreme Court ruling. But that money went to businesses, not directly to ordinary Americans.

In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has made promises of more cash payments. During his speech at the Republican National Committee midterm convention in September, the US president said US adults would receive a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if his party “wins” next month’s elections.

Polling indicates that proposal has backfired, with 45 percent of unaffiliated voters telling NBC News they would be less likely to support a candidate who’s in agreement with it.

But it plays well — extremely well, even — with Trump’s base, whose members believe they’re entitled to a form of compensation from the government.

“I think it’s great if the president can help all people that need it,” Lashley said. “I mean, we got the money. We all contributed in our life to our country.”

“I paid tax all my life. I deserve something back”, Ott said. “They never give me nothing.”

Lashley stood up and replied, “That’s right!”

‘They’re taking everything’

Most Americans say Trump’s economic policies have burdened, rather than benefitted, them.

About seven in 10 Americans, including more than half of Republicans, believe his handling of the cost of living has been “worse than expected”, according to the AP poll.

But MAGA voters say they are sticking firmly with the president, even as his economic agenda faces growing criticism across the country.

To understand why his most hardcore supporters remain loyal, it is important to understand how Trump built his political coalition in the first place.

A study by New America found that Trump’s coalition has been closely bound and heavily driven by resentment towards opposing cultural and political groups. Lashley reflected that sentiment when she blamed immigrants for the country’s cost-of-living crisis.

“They’re taking over the businesses in our country. They’re taking everything,” she said. “I’m not on board with giving people who come here more than what we get. No!”

Lashley went even further, saying she wished Trump could remain president for the rest of his life.

“I wish he could be our president until he died,” she said. “What is going to happen when he’s gone? That’s what really worries me.”

“I trust Trump with my life,” Ott said.

Rising prices alone have not been enough to sever the bond between Trump and some of his most loyal voters.

For many of them, the choice is not simply between an expensive economy and a cheaper one. It is about what – and who – might come after Trump.

“I’m afraid that somebody’s going to get in there that’s not gonna do the job, and then we’re gonna go downhill again,” Ott said. “I worry about the Democrats”.

“Me too. They’re crazy,” Lashley replied.

“What they’re gonna do to this country. We’re gonna be suffering,” Ott said. “We might as well be living in South Africa or somewhere like that.”

That loyalty could prove important in November.

In this year’s Republican primaries, Trump has demonstrated that the GOP primary electorate will follow his lead. A string of victories by candidates he endorsed in the US states of Indiana, Kentucky and Texas has further solidified his grip on the party.

While the president’s political instinct for activating his loyal, but often low-propensity, voters in critical elections has generally been effective, it is less clear whether they can hold back a rising wave of Democratic support.

Progressive and liberal-leaning candidates have coalesced around a message of affordability and lower prices – an approach that has resonated with voters who feel increasingly squeezed by Trump’s policies.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in August showed that US voters gave Democrats a 36 to 28 percent advantage over Republicans on cost-of-living issues.

While Lashley acknowledged that the issue resonated with her, she said there were no circumstances in which she would consider voting against the president.

More than 70 percent of US voters who identify with MAGA indicated in a September PBS News/NPR/Marist poll that they were voting in this election to support Trump.

For Williams, who said he plans to vote a straight Republican ticket in November, the economy is not his priority. The choice, he said, boils down to a battle he described as good versus evil.

“Look at the s*** that they’re trying to shove down our kids’ throats with these drag shows and the gender changes,” Williams vented as he described some Democrats’ positions on transgender rights. “Now I don’t know about you, but that’s evil right there. And I have a huge problem with that.”

But Ott said he was sticking with Republicans because of his optimism that economic conditions in the US would improve during the second half of the president’s term.

“[Trump] is gonna do more,” he said. “This economy is going to be so much better.”

entries.title: ‘Not getting involved’: US Vice President refuses to endorse Netanyahu
entries.summary: JD Vance's comments follow Donald Trump's backing of Israeli prime minister ahead of October 27 elections.
entries.content:
JD Vance’s comments follow Donald Trump’s backing of Israeli prime minister ahead of October 27 elections.

United States Vice President JD Vance has declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of elections this month, saying he would prefer to stay on the sidelines and focus on midterm polls in the US.

Vance’s comments during an interview on Monday with journalist Mark Halperin came just a day after US President Donald Trump explicitly endorsed Netanyahu.

“I’m not anti-endorsing him. I’m not pro-endorsing him. I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

“I endorse American candidates and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterms,” he added.

Vance last threw his weight behind a foreign leader in April, when he backed Hungary’s former right-wing Prime Minister Victor Orban, who lost in a landslide to Peter Magyar.

Over his two terms, Trump has cultivated a close relationship with Netanyahu and his right-wing government.

In his first term, Trump moved the US embassy to west Jerusalem, recognised Israel’s annexation of the Golan Heights, withdrew from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and spearheaded a series of normalisation agreements with Arab countries that sidelined the Israel-Palestine issue.

Since taking office again in January 2025, the Trump administration has continued to sell weapons to Israel despite its genocidal war on Gaza, entered a conflict with Iran and escalated a crackdown on the International Criminal Court (ICC).

For his part, Vance, considered a likely 2028 presidential contender, has become emblematic of growing discontent within the Republican party over Washington’s unconditional support for Israel. That sentiment has deepened with the impact of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has raised costs for US consumers.

While the vice president has said US support for Israel should continue, he has faced scepticism from Jewish Republicans about his commitment to the alliance.

In June, amid Israeli opposition to an Iran ceasefire plan, Vance told Israel: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have”.

He also warned Netanyahu’s cabinet against alienating Trump, calling the president “the only powerful ally” Israel has left.

It remains unclear whether Trump’s endorsement will boost Netanyahu’s Likud party ahead of the vote, with some opinion polls indicating wariness of the US president over his perceived attempts to restrain Israeli operations in Lebanon and resistance to further escalation in Iran.

Polls have shown the Yashar party leading Likud ahead of the October 27 vote. Its leader, former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, has said he will seek to build an opposition bloc to form a government.

entries.title: Eastern Libya parliament approves 2019 maritime deal with Turkiye
entries.summary: The vote recognises Ankara's maritime deal with Tripoli, ending Haftar's 2020 boycott.
entries.content:
The vote recognises Ankara’s maritime deal with Tripoli, ending Haftar’s 2020 boycott.

Libya’s eastern-based parliament, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, which runs as an alternative to the UN-recognised legislature in Tripoli, has approved a maritime deal with Turkiye, ending years of acrimony.

Haftar’s Benghazi-based government said in a statement on Tuesday that his Tobruk-based House of Representatives voted unanimously to approve the 2019 memorandum of understanding signed between Turkiye and Libya’s UN-recognised former Government of National Accord (GNA) on the delimitation of maritime boundaries between the two countries in the Mediterranean Sea.

Specialised committees presented a full and detailed explanation of the deal’s provisions, lawmaker Aisha al-Tabalqi told the Reuters news agency.

The approval came six years after the same parliament ⁠in 2020 unanimously rejected the ratification of the deal and cut political ties with Ankara.

Strategic shift

The repealing of those moves on Tuesday consolidates a strategic shift in the works since last year, building on Ankara’s military-to-military contacts with Haftar’s self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), including a deal in July to develop military facilities and advanced surveillance systems.

The LNA, long believed to have been supported by Egypt and other regional powers, has been in conflict with forces loyal to the Tripoli-based government since the start of the Libyan civil war in 2014.

In 2019, Turkiye signed an agreement with the Tripoli-based government delineating the maritime boundaries between the two countries in the Mediterranean, triggering protests from Greece and Cyprus.

Both European countries denounced the agreement, saying it was a serious breach of international law that disregarded the rights of other eastern Mediterranean countries.

“Some countries may be upset by this ⁠agreement, but what matters to us is our national interest,” said Tarek al-Jeroushi, a lawmaker in the eastern-backed parliament, adding that the ⁠agreement would strengthen Libya’s position as a political, military and economic partner to key powers.

In December 2019, Haftar’s LNA had nearly encircled Tripoli, threatening to overrun the

UN-recognised GNA, which at the time was led by Fayez al-Sarraj, before Turkiye decided to intervene, sending military advisers and drones to stop the LNA, and altering the trajectory of the Libyan civil war.

Seven years later, there is talk of Ankara setting up a military presence in areas under the control of Haftar’s LNA.

This eastern pivot is designed to secure Turkiye’s long-term geopolitical and economic interests, preserving its influence in Libya regardless of future political settlements between the government and eastern authorities.

entries.title: Yemen’s Taiz faces deadly siege, as Shabwah death toll rises
entries.summary: Government forces launch major offensives across multiple Yemeni front lines as a tightening blockade threatens Taiz.
entries.content:
Government forces launch major offensives across multiple Yemeni front lines as the tightening blockade on Taiz threatens millions of Yemenis.

The siege on Taiz has cut humanitarian supplies to the Yemeni city, the United Nations has warned, and left many of its inhabitants without food and other essentials.

UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk said on Tuesday that the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), who have surrounded the city, must immediately allow humanitarian relief to enter or risk a catastrophe.

“The Houthis’ closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies,” the high commissioner said.

“Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated. Civilians wishing to leave must be allowed to do so freely and safely.”

Besieged city

Taiz, which has been repeatedly besieged throughout the war, has been encircled again by the Houthis after they captured a major road linking the city to southern Yemen.

The humanitarian situation in Taiz is reaching a breaking point with the prices of basic commodities multiplying in price, amid shortages of some goods.

Continued fighting in Taiz governorate has also killed at least 32 civilians between August 1 and October 19, including 14 children. There are fears of more deaths as fighting approaches the city.

“I urge all parties to the conflict to refrain from the use of explosive weapons with wide-area effects in populated areas and to take all feasible precautions to protect civilians and civilian objects,” Turk said.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government had appealed to the United Nations to intervene and lift the blockade, warning that the Houthi siege threatens more than 4 million people.

The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that shifting front lines and road closures have cut off 800,000 people from life-saving assistance, the vast majority located in Taiz. Nationwide, more than 18 million Yemenis face severe food insecurity.

Forces aligned with the internationally-recognised government on Monday launched air strikes in Taiz governorate that destroyed Houthi reinforcements in Najd Qasim and a weapons depot in Jabal Habashi.

Shabwa attack

On Tuesday, local authorities raised the death toll from a Houthi attack on a military base in Shabwa governorate to 73.

Monday’s Houthi ballistic missile strikes on al-Alam camp were condemned by the Yemeni government as a “treacherous bloody assault” and a war crime.

President of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi formally requested the UN to designate the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation”.

The United Kingdom said on Tuesday it would deploy fighter jets to help protect Saudi Arabia from attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, after cities and infrastructure were targeted in rocket and drone attacks.

The British Ministry of Defence said that Typhoon warplanes would play a “defensive role” only and would not carry out attacks in Yemen.

Egypt’s parliament meanwhile delayed a vote on Monday to authorise the military to support Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis.

Ali al-Dahab, a military and security strategic affairs expert, said that while there appears to be more international support for the anti-Houthi alliance, this will not likely translate into boots on the ground in Yemen.

“The probability of international ground forces engaging to confront the Houthis seems slim; expected participation will be limited to air and naval support,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Yemeni military launched a sweeping offensive dubbed “Dawn of Yemen” on 5 October to reverse recent Houthi advances. But despite initial successes in the early days of the campaign, with hundreds of Houthi fighters reportedly killed in air strikes, there are questions about whether these counter-offensives have run out of steam.

“The transition from defence to offence remains limited on the ground, and the map of the Yemeni government’s influence in al-Marib [an energy-rich part of central Yemen] has not expanded to the extent implied by the meaning of the [operation],” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.

“Government forces must exploit the gaps created by conventional and drone air strikes in Houthi ranks by launching a multi-directional operation that turns this into a strategic shift, specifically in the northwestern direction toward Sanaa.”

Cross-border strikes

The intensification of ground battles in Yemen has triggered a wave of cross-border attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi-led coalition said Tuesday it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh. The attack prompted the Saudi Civil Defense to activate early warning platforms across the capital.

The Arab coalition has launched waves of strikes on Houthi positions across Yemen during the past week.

“On the strategic and long-term, [aerial attrition strikes] can have a tangible impact on the Houthis’ military infrastructure, structures, machines, and vehicles,” al-Dahab said.

However, he questioned the government’s ability to capitalise on these strikes on the western coast, where the Yemeni government is attempting to claw back losses from the Houthis.

“Do government forces have enough power to launch an attack toward Mocha on the coast or toward Hodeidah?” al-Dahab asked, noting that Houthi fighters are desperately holding onto the Kahboub mountains in Lahij for their commanding maritime view over the Gulf of Aden and the southern Red Sea.
